sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Yellowknife homes
sections.html:
Of Yellowknife's 5,225 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 3% were built before 1961 and 57% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical Yellowknife house dates from 1981–1990, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Yellowknife gets about 7,856 heating degree-days a year, a measure of how much heating its climate needs, and its winter design temperature, the cold day heating systems are sized for, is −39.2°C. Those figures come from the climate data for Yellowknife in HOT2000, the home-energy software Natural Resources Canada (NRCan) gives energy advisors. That's the highest heating demand of the 70 cities we cover. Extreme cold and a very long heating season: envelope work comes first, and heating reliability is a safety issue.

Wildfire smoke reaches Yellowknife in some summers. The Government of Canada's advice is to keep windows and doors closed, limit exhaust fans and use the best filter your system can handle, so ask the advisor what your furnace or HRV can take.
The Arctic Energy Alliance delivers subsidized EnerGuide evaluations: $200 + GST for a single-family existing home.

sections.h2: How a home energy assessment (EnerGuide evaluation) works

• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.

glance.note: The cold day heating is sized for
Extreme cold, very long winters

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Yellowknife
sections.html:
−39.2°C is the 1st-coldest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −39.2°C, even cold-climate heat pumps lose capacity just when you need heat most. The room-by-room number tells you how much the heat pump can cover and how much backup heat to plan for, rather than guessing from square footage.

The National Building Code 2020 requires the heating capacity for a house to be worked out with CSA F280, and its list of referenced documents names the 2012 edition, CSA F280-12. Provincial codes can name their own edition and climate values, so ask your designer which ones the calculation uses.

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

faq.q: What is ductwork pressure testing?

faq.q: Should I close vents in unused rooms?

sections.h2: Why Yellowknife homes get humidity problems
sections.html:
Yellowknife gets about 7,856 heating degree-days a year, a measure of how much heating its climate needs, and its winter design temperature, the cold day heating systems are sized for, is −39.2°C. Those figures come from the climate data for Yellowknife in HOT2000, the home-energy software Natural Resources Canada (NRCan) gives energy advisors. On Yellowknife's coldest days, window glass and poorly insulated corners get cold enough for condensation at humidity levels that feel normal indoors, so winter humidity needs to stay at the lower end of the comfortable range.

Of Yellowknife's 5,225 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 3% were built before 1961 and 57% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Newer houses (22% of Yellowknife's were built since 2001) are tight and usually have an HRV or ERV that needs balancing and cleaning. Older houses that get air-sealed can lose the accidental ventilation they used to rely on.

Wildfire smoke reaches Yellowknife in some summers. The Government of Canada's advice is to keep windows and doors closed, limit exhaust fans and use the best filter your system can handle, so ask the advisor what your furnace or HRV can take. radon-testing.h1: Radon testing and long-term monitoring in Yellowknife
radon-testing.title: Radon testing in Yellowknife: long-term monitoring, kits and mitigation
radon-testing.description: Radon in Yellowknife: Health Canada survey results for the Northwest Territories region (5.4% above the guideline), how to run a 91-day long-term test, digital monitors versus alpha-track kits, and mitigation by C-NRPP professionals ($2,000–$3,000).
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 5.4% of homes tested in the Northwest Territories health region were above the guideline, and only a long-term test tells you about your own house.

glance.note: Neighbours' results don't predict yours: test
Health Canada's level for fixing a home

sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 5.4% of 185 homes tested in the Northwest Territories health region above the guideline.

No survey can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely. Testing is the only way to know.

sections.h2: Long-term monitoring: how to test properly
sections.html:
Health Canada's measurement guide asks for a long-term test with at least 91 days in the heating season, when closed windows and the stack effect make readings higher, so the result is a conservative estimate of the yearly average. It recommends testing for 3 to 12 months. Our radon testing guide walks through each step.

Place the detector on the lowest level where someone spends more than four hours a day, at least 30 cm above the floor and 30 cm from walls, and at least 1 m from vents, windows and doors; avoid kitchens, laundry rooms and bathrooms. The choice of device:

  • Alpha track detectors record radon's alpha particles on a plastic film; you mail them to a lab when the test ends. A long-term kit costs about $30–$80 including the lab fee (Windsor-Essex County Health Unit).
  • Electret ion chambers lose charge as radon ionizes the air inside; a lab reads the voltage drop.
  • Digital (electronic) monitors read continuously and show results on a screen or an app, and cost more (Lung Saskatchewan sells one for $189). For a long-term test, Health Canada says to use one that has passed C-NRPP performance testing, and it still has to run at least three months.
  • Continuous monitoring after mitigation: a digital monitor left running lets you watch for changes between the follow-up long-term tests Health Canada recommends.

• We found no NWT radon program; long-term kits can be ordered from lung associations.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your Yellowknife postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

sections.h2: If your level is high: mitigation
sections.html:
Health Canada recommends fixing levels above 200 Bq/m³ within a year, and sooner the higher the level. The usual fix is a sub-slab depressurization system (a sealed pipe through the floor and a fan venting outside), which Health Canada says costs about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour and cuts radon by more than 80% in most homes. Hire a professional certified for mitigation under C-NRPP. After a system goes in:

  • A C-NRPP professional runs a short test starting at least 24 hours after the fan is turned on.
  • A long-term three-month test follows in the next fall or winter, done by a company other than the installer.
  • With an active system, Health Canada recommends a long-term test within two years of activation and every five years after that, and again after renovations.
  • Check the system's pressure gauge (manometer) regularly and never switch the fan off. It costs about $50 to $75 a year to run; a replacement fan is $200 to $300.

sections.h2: Rules and help in Northwest Territories
sections.html: • The NWT adopted the 2020 National Building Code in full (enforced October 1, 2024), including its radon rough-in for new homes.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in Yellowknife?
faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 5.4% of 185 homes tested in the Northwest Territories health region above the guideline. Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least 91 days, in the heating season. Health Canada recommends 3 to 12 months; short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in Yellowknife?
faq.a: We found no NWT radon program; long-term kits can be ordered from lung associations. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits, for about $30–$80 including the lab fee.

faq.q: Digital radon monitor or alpha-track kit?
faq.a: An alpha-track kit is the cheaper long-term test: it sits for three months or more and goes to a lab. A digital monitor shows readings as it goes and can keep running after mitigation; for a long-term result, use one that has passed C-NRPP testing and run it for at least three months.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Health Canada puts a sub-slab depressurization system at about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour, plus about $50 to $75 a year to run the fan. Hire a C-NRPP-certified mitigation professional.

faq.q: Should I keep monitoring after mitigation?
faq.a: Yes. Health Canada recommends a long-term test in the following heating season, another within two years of activation, and one every five years after that. A digital monitor running in between shows if anything changes.

sections.h2: Where CO alarms go: installation rules in Northwest Territories

  • For new houses, the National Building Code 2020 (Article 9.32.3.9) requires a CO alarm inside each bedroom or within 5 m outside each bedroom door when the home has a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage, an alarm in any room with a solid-fuel-burning appliance (on or near the ceiling unless the maker's instructions say otherwise), and interconnected alarms in a house with a secondary suite.

There's no piped natural gas for homes in Yellowknife, so the usual CO sources are oil furnaces, propane appliances, wood stoves and attached garages.

Single-detached houses make up 44% of Yellowknife's households; many have an attached garage, another reason to put an alarm near the door into the house.

• Alarms next to sleeping areas and on every storey, tested monthly and replaced by their end-of-life date (usually 7 to 10 years).
  • Annual service of fuel-burning appliances by a licensed technician.
  • A combustion spillage test during an energy evaluation, which catches a venting problem before it produces CO.

mold-testing.h1: Mould and indoor air quality testing in Yellowknife
mold-testing.title: Mould and indoor air quality (IAQ) testing in Yellowknife: air sampling, inspection and remediation
mold-testing.description: Mould inspection and indoor air quality testing in Yellowknife: when mold sampling is worth it, why cold winters cause condensation, the CMHC and Health Canada size rules for cleanup, and when to hire a remediation contractor.
mold-testing.lede: Mould sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mould problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure. Here's how to inspect a home in Yellowknife, when air quality testing helps, and how much cleanup you can safely do yourself.

glance.note: Older basements and walls have more damp spots

glance.sub: or if it keeps coming back

glance.note: Ask which accredited lab reads the samples

sections.h2: Why mould shows up in Yellowknife homes
sections.html:
Yellowknife gets about 7,856 heating degree-days a year, a measure of how much heating its climate needs, and its winter design temperature, the cold day heating systems are sized for, is −39.2°C. Those figures come from the climate data for Yellowknife in HOT2000, the home-energy software Natural Resources Canada (NRCan) gives energy advisors. On cold days, exterior corners, closets on outside walls and window frames get cold enough for condensation, which is where mould usually starts in Yellowknife houses.

Of Yellowknife's 5,225 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 3% were built before 1961 and 57% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

sections.h2: Mould inspection: when sampling is worth it
sections.html:
Start by looking and smelling: stains, discoloured patches, peeling paint and a musty odour, especially in basements, bathrooms, window frames and closets on outside walls. Health Canada says measuring mould concentrations or identifying species is usually unnecessary.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

Air or surface sampling helps in three cases:

  • You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

sections.h2: Cleanup and remediation: the size rules
sections.html:
CMHC and Health Canada sort mould by size, and the size decides who should clean it up:

SizeWhat countsWho should clean it
SmallOne to three patches, each smaller than 1 m²A healthy homeowner, with water and unscented dish detergent (CMHC)
MediumMore than three patches, or patches between 1 and 3 m² (32 square feet)Trained help; homeowners only with training and precautions
LargeA patch larger than 3 m², or many patches through the houseA qualified mould remediation contractor (CMHC)
  • Fix the moisture source first: a leak, poor drainage, or condensation from high humidity. Health Canada recommends 30–50% relative humidity.
  • For a small cleanup, wear safety glasses or goggles, an N95 mask if possible and household rubber gloves. People at risk from mould shouldn't clean it and should stay away.
  • Health Canada suggests professional help for extensive mould, especially growth that keeps coming back after cleaning.

sections.h2: Choosing a tester, lab or remediation contractor
sections.html:
Ask any Yellowknife tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause. For remediation, get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the area is cleaned.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in Yellowknife · Our mould and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: How much does mould testing cost in Yellowknife?
faq.a: We found no reputable Canadian source for the cost of a professional mould assessment, so get two or three written quotes and ask how many samples are included, which lab analyzes them and what the report covers.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: How much mould can I clean myself?
faq.a: CMHC says a healthy homeowner can clean one to three patches, each under 1 m², with water and unscented dish detergent. Larger areas need trained help or a remediation contractor.

faq.q: When should I hire a mould remediation contractor?
faq.a: For a single patch over 3 m², many patches through the house, or mould that keeps coming back after cleaning (CMHC, Health Canada).

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

asbestos-testing.lede: About 3,000 Yellowknife houses (57%) were built before 1991, when asbestos still turned up in insulation, flooring, plaster and duct wrap. A lab test before renovation is the only way to know.

glance.note: Asbestos still turned up in materials until then
Have it sampled before attic work

sections.h2: Where asbestos shows up in Yellowknife houses
sections.html:
Of Yellowknife's 5,225 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 3% were built before 1961 and 57% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.
  • Vinyl floor tiles and their adhesive, textured ceilings and some plaster.
  • Duct wrap and pipe insulation on older heating systems.

The NWT's Asbestos Abatement Code of Practice calls a building survey an important step before renovating or demolishing pre-1980 buildings, and asbestos waste must be handled as hazardous waste.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program.

Our asbestos and vermiculite guide · Attic inspections in Yellowknife

sections.h2: If it's positive: abatement and removal
sections.html:
Leave the material alone until a plan is in place. For vermiculite, Health Canada says not to use the attic for storage, to keep children out and to seal gaps around the attic hatch, light fixtures and outlets, and to hire professionals trained to handle asbestos if you plan to renovate.

In Northwest Territories: WSCC's Asbestos Abatement Code of Practice sets the requirements for the work, and asbestos waste must be managed as hazardous waste in sealed, impervious containers.

Abatement is quoted separately from testing. Get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the waste will be disposed of.

faq.q: Do I need an asbestos test before renovating in Yellowknife?
faq.a: If the house was built before 1991 and the work will disturb insulation, flooring, plaster or duct wrap, test first. The NWT's Asbestos Abatement Code of Practice calls a building survey an important step before renovating or demolishing pre-1980 buildings, and asbestos waste must be handled as hazardous waste.

faq.q: How much does asbestos testing cost?
faq.a: About $50–$150 per lab sample, plus the assessor's visit. Abatement, if needed, is quoted separately.

faq.q: What should I do if I have vermiculite in the attic?
faq.a: Leave it alone, keep the attic closed, and have it sampled before any attic work. Health Canada advises against disturbing it or removing it yourself.

faq.q: Who removes asbestos in Northwest Territories?
faq.a: WSCC's Asbestos Abatement Code of Practice sets the requirements for the work, and asbestos waste must be managed as hazardous waste in sealed, impervious containers.

lead-paint-testing.title: Lead paint testing in Yellowknife: at-risk homes, testing and safe abatement
lead-paint-testing.description: 3% of Yellowknife's houses were built before 1961, when lead paint was common. How to test with $15–$40 swabs or a lab, and how to renovate safely.
lead-paint-testing.lede: Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably has lead paint somewhere. That's 3% of Yellowknife's houses (built before 1961, per the 2021 Census), plus exterior paint on many of the 54% built from 1961 to 1990.

glance.note: Probably has lead paint somewhere (Health Canada)
Exterior paint may contain lead
A quick screen, not proof

sections.h2: Which Yellowknife homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of Yellowknife's 5,225 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 3% were built before 1961 and 57% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

sections.h2: If it's positive: lead paint abatement
sections.html:
Health Canada says leaving lead-based paint alone is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach, and covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling adds protection. Paint that's chipping, flaking or within reach of children is a serious hazard and has to come off carefully; consider hiring an expert before you start.

No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. must include lead in pre-renovation and demolition hazard inspections, and in Yukon before demolition. If you do the work yourself, Health Canada's precautions are:

  • Don't use sanders, heat guns or blowlamps: they create toxic dust and fumes. For do-it-yourself work, Health Canada suggests a chemical paint-stripper paste applied with a brush.
  • Move furniture out or cover it with plastic, seal doorways and vents with plastic sheeting and tape, and run a fan blowing out through an open window.
  • Wear goggles, gloves and a good-quality mask, work in 10-minute stretches with breaks outdoors, and don't eat, drink or smoke in the work area.
  • Clean up daily: put scrapings in a sealed container marked Hazardous Waste, follow your municipality's disposal instructions, and wipe surfaces with a damp cloth you throw away.
  • Keep children and pregnant people away until the work is done; Health Canada says there is no known safe level of lead exposure.

faq.q: Does my Yellowknife house have lead paint?
faq.a: If it was built before 1960, probably; 1960–1990, possibly on the exterior. Test the surfaces you plan to disturb.

faq.q: Are lead test swabs reliable?
faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

faq.q: What does lead paint testing cost?
faq.a: Swab kits run about $15–$40; lab analysis and XRF testing cost more and are quoted by the firm.

faq.q: Should I remove lead paint or cover it?
faq.a: Health Canada says leaving it alone or covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach. Never sand it or use a heat gun, and consider hiring an expert for removal.

well-water-testing.title: Well water testing in Yellowknife: bacteria (E. coli and total coliform) tests and costs in Northwest Territories
well-water-testing.description: Private well water testing in Yellowknife: most homes are on city water, but some rely on wells. How Northwest Territories's bacteria testing for E. coli and total coliforms works, what it costs and how often to test.
well-water-testing.lede: About 680 Yellowknife residents (roughly 4%) receive the City's trucked water and most others are on its piped system, so private household wells are rare. If yours is, here's how testing works in Northwest Territories.

glance.note: These tests matter only if your home has a well
E. coli and total coliforms

sections.html:
About 680 Yellowknife residents (roughly 4%) receive the City's trucked water and most others are on its piped system, so private household wells are rare.

Local program: The GNWT's Taiga Environmental Laboratory in Yellowknife accepts samples from private citizens (fee-based; bottles free). Details

sections.h2: How testing works in Northwest Territories
sections.html: There's no free program: the GNWT's Taiga Environmental Laboratory in Yellowknife tests private samples ($28 for bacteria in its 2021 price guide) and supplies bottles free.

• Bacteria (total coliforms and E. coli): at least once a year, and after flooding, heavy rain or work on the well.
  • Nitrate, especially near farmland or septic systems.
  • Metals and naturally occurring contaminants such as arsenic, uranium or manganese when a well is new and every few years after, depending on local geology.

Our well water guide.

faq.q: Is well water testing free in Northwest Territories?
faq.a: There's no free program: the GNWT's Taiga Environmental Laboratory in Yellowknife tests private samples ($28 for bacteria in its 2021 price guide) and supplies bottles free.

faq.q: How often should I test my well?
faq.a: For bacteria, at least once a year and after flooding, heavy rain or well work; many health units recommend more often. Test chemistry when the well is new and every few years after.

faq.q: Are private wells common in Yellowknife?
faq.a: About 680 Yellowknife residents (roughly 4%) receive the City's trucked water and most others are on its piped system, so private household wells are rare.

commercial-energy-audit.title: Commercial energy audits in Yellowknife: reporting rules and incentives
commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in Yellowknife: ASHRAE levels, no mandatory reporting rule, and 1 utility or government incentive for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in Yellowknife: no mandatory reporting rule and 1 incentive program we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in Yellowknife
sections.html: • No city-specific rule found (none found): No municipal energy/water benchmarking, reporting or building-performance by-law found; provincial rules apply (see rules.provinces.NT).

• Building Improvements - building energy audits (Arctic Energy Alliance (NWT)): Free desktop 'yardstick' audits (utility bill analysis) and free on-site targeted audits (heating, ventilation, air leakage, water equipment, lighting) for businesses and non-profits; community governments pay a fee but may get a $15,000 subsidy. Upgrade rebates up to $50,000 (up to $75,000 for community and Indigenous governments and Indigenous development corporations), the lower of 50% of eligible costs or a savings-based calculation. Details

• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.

faq.q: Do Yellowknife buildings have to report energy use?
faq.a: We found no mandatory reporting rule for Yellowknife buildings as of September 28, 2026.

faq.q: Are there incentives for commercial energy audits in Yellowknife?
faq.a: Yes: Building Improvements - building energy audits. Check eligibility and pre-approval rules before you commission the audit.

faq.q: What does a commercial energy audit cost?
faq.a: It depends on the building's size and the ASHRAE level. Get quotes that state the level and the deliverables.
